title: The Less Active Input Is Removed

scenes.tts: A newborn rat muscle fiber is wired to two or more motor neurons. Nothing is wrong with the extra inputs. Each one releases acetylcholine, and each one makes the fiber respond. In the adult, each fiber has one junction and one axon. Within two to three weeks, the fiber listens to just one. Where do the extra inputs go? And who decides which one stays?
scenes.visual: A muscle fiber with two colored axons ending on its receptor sites; pulses run down both and the receptors light up; then one input is left and question marks sit over both axons.
scenes.narration: A newborn rat muscle fiber is wired to two or more motor neurons. Nothing is wrong with the extra inputs. Each one releases acetylcholine, and each one makes the fiber respond. In the adult, each fiber has one junction and one axon. Within two to three weeks, the fiber listens to just one. Where do the extra inputs go? And who decides which one stays?

scenes.tts: First, did the extra neurons die? That would explain the loss. But in rat soleus muscle, the number of motor neurons did not change significantly. Yet by the end of the second week, nearly every fiber had one input. Both facts are true only if each surviving neuron pulled back some of its branches. Losing an input means losing a branch, not a cell.
scenes.visual: Two motor neurons branch to four fibers; a red neuron-death question is crossed out while the neuron count stays at two; branches retract until each fiber has one input.
scenes.narration: First, did the extra neurons die? That would explain the loss. But in rat soleus muscle, the number of motor neurons did not change significantly. scenes.tts: Now watch one junction over days, in mouse pups. Each axon glows in its own color, and the receptor sites are labeled too. Typically, one axon withdraws from the sites. The other extends into the sites it left. The movie looks like a takeover. And the winner could not be reliably predicted from how much territory each axon held at the start.
scenes.visual: Six receptor sites, blue axon on three, orange on three; blue beads vanish one by one while orange slides into each; then territory-at-start with a crossed-out arrow to winner.
scenes.narration: Now watch one junction over days, in mouse pups. Each axon glows in its own color, and the receptor sites are labeled too. Typically, one axon withdraws from the sites. The other extends into the sites it left. The movie looks like a takeover. And the winner could not be reliably predicted from how much territory each axon held at the start.

scenes.tts: So what shapes the contest? Activity. In newborn rat muscle, blocking nerve impulses slows elimination. Stimulating the muscle sometimes speeds it up. But these tests changed activity everywhere at once. They could not tell whether the loser is silent, or only less active than its neighbor.
scenes.visual: Yellow pulses run down both axons; blocked, they stop and the label says slower; stimulated, they stream and the label says faster; a box around everything; two candidate rules appear as chips.
scenes.narration: So what shapes the contest? Activity. In newborn rat muscle, blocking nerve impulses slows elimination. Stimulating the muscle sometimes speeds it up. But these tests changed activity everywhere at once. They could not tell whether the loser is silent, or only less active than its neighbor.

scenes.tts: Here is a test, in adult mice. A toxin, alpha bungarotoxin, binds acetylcholine receptors and blocks them. Block one patch of a junction. The receptors there are lost, and the nerve terminal withdraws from that patch. Now block the whole junction. Nothing is eliminated.

scenes.visual: Two junctions side by side; in the left one a single receptor patch turns red, then the receptors and terminal there vanish; in the right one all receptors turn red and nothing is lost.
scenes.narration: Here is a test, in adult mice. A toxin, alpha-bungarotoxin, binds acetylcholine receptors and blocks them. Block one patch of a junction. The receptors there are lost, and the nerve terminal withdraws from that patch. Now block the whole junction. Nothing is eliminated.

scenes.tts: Why? With a partial block, a silent patch sits next to active patches. With a full block, every site is equally silent. Nothing is less active than its neighbor. Active sites can destabilize inactive synapses nearby, over a short distance within one junction. Keep this rule. A less active synapse is more likely to go.
scenes.visual: The two blocked junctions again: yellow activity on the unblocked sites beside the silent patch; red arrows from active sites to the silent one; none in the full block; ends on the rule in large type.
